extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing fiction writers (novelists and short-story writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on composing, resting, revising, and soliciting feedback for fiction (novels and short stories), emphasizing draft-phases, pacing, backstory, research, and reader-feedback strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write the first draft with the door shut
rubrics_metrics.description: Write the first draft 'with the door shut' so you concentrate on story to the exclusion of practically everything else; don’t worry about what readers or critics will ask later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid analyzing symbolism, themes, or trying to be 'wonderful' in the first draft. Focus on telling the story; resist outside questions like 'what were you trying to express with X?' until later drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-draft rest period (minimum six weeks)
rubrics_metrics.description: After finishing a first draft, give the manuscript a period of rest (the author advises a minimum of six weeks) before returning to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put the manuscript away in a drawer and work on something else (shorter, different project) so your imagination can recycle. Resist re-reading or tinkering during this cooling-off period to avoid premature revisions based on temporary impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: First re-read: read straight through (one sitting if possible)
rubrics_metrics.description: When you return to the manuscript after the rest, read it straight through (all in one sitting if feasible) with a pencil and legal pad to make notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrate on mundane housekeeping (misspellings, inconsistencies), mark pages needing cuts/changes, and note larger problems to address in the second draft. Make big-picture as well as line-level notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Housekeeping/line-level edits on re-read
rubrics_metrics.description: During the re-read focus on housekeeping jobs: fixing misspellings, picking up inconsistencies, clarifying unclear antecedents, adding clarifying phrases, and deleting adverbs where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be anal-retentive about small errors—only a slob says 'let it go, that's what copyeditors are for.' Specifically: distrust pronouns with unclear antecedents; delete all adverbs you can bear to part with (not necessarily all).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask the Big Questions (coherence, theme, resonance)
rubrics_metrics.description: On revision, ask whether the story is coherent, what will make coherence sing, what the recurring elements are, whether they entwine to make a theme, and how to achieve resonance without spoon-feeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify 'What’s it all about?' and use the second draft to add scenes that reinforce the meaning and delete material that goes in other directions. Aim for lingering resonance rather than explicit moralizing or message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and fix glaring structural holes (character motivation, plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for 'holes big enough to drive a truck through'—particularly errors in character motivation and major plot gaps—during the reread and revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark pages that need cuts or changes and don’t beat yourself up for screw-ups; fix them systematically. Example: note a scene where a character’s action is inconsistent with established motivation and either explain or alter the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an Ideal Reader as a mental and actual audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a single Ideal Reader (a specific person in mind) whom you are writing for; this reader lives in your head during composition and becomes the real first reader when you open the door.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Ideal Reader helps you judge tone, pacing, and emotional beats while writing. When selecting first readers, give special weight to the person who most closely matches your Ideal Reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show the manuscript to a small, trusted set of readers (door open phase)
rubrics_metrics.description: After self-revision, show the work to four to eight close friends/critics who have agreed to read and to wait before discussing it until you are ready.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose readers you respect; some will specialize in factual catches, some in subjective response. Gather their opinions to determine where problems persist. Ensure they promise not to discuss the book until you ask.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight reader feedback intelligently (consensus matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all opinions are equal: if multiple readers independently point out the same problem, treat it as a real issue that needs fixing; when opinions are split, the tie goes to the writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay most attention to your Ideal Reader’s responses. If everyone says 'this part is a problem' you have a problem. If some like A and others like B, you can safely favor your instincts (tie goes to the writer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specialist first-readers for factual verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask at least one knowledgeable reader to catch factual or technical errors (e.g., weapon calibers, procedures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialist readers provide both the error and often the fix, making your work more credible and flattering the reader. Example: a reader corrected a mistaken caliber attribution in a manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware revising to please test-audiences; use trusted feedback instead
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid revising your novel based on mass test screenings or general demographics; limited trusted readers are different and useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test-screening-style revisions can dumb down or homogenize work. Rely on a few knowledgeable, trustworthy readers (not a multiplex audience) when making substantive changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing: match pace to story and reader tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: Pace is the speed at which narrative unfolds. Choose a pace appropriate to the story—neither so fast you lose the reader nor so slow you bore them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the tastes of your Ideal Reader to judge whether a scene is too slow or too chatty. Use cutting to increase pace when necessary (Elmore Leonard: 'leave out the boring parts'). Beware both over-acceleration and over-slowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite for concision (Rewrite Formula: 2nd Draft = 1st Draft -10%)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply a rule-of-thumb to tighten prose: aim to reduce length in the second draft (example formula cited: 2nd Draft = 1st Draft - 10%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice ruthless cutting (kill your darlings) to sharpen pace and clarity. The author gives concrete targets: e.g., trim ~10% between drafts; this often yields immediate, positive effect on reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backstory belongs in the background and should be graceful
rubrics_metrics.description: Backstory is what happened before the front story; it should be included as needed, as far in the background as possible, and introduced gracefully rather than by clumsy info-dumps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid blunt exposition lines (example: 'Hello, ex-wife'). Instead, reveal past through small, graceful details that clarify motivation. Stick to interesting portions of backstory and cut the rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit research to providing verisimilitude; story and characters come first
rubrics_metrics.description: Research is a specialized kind of backstory; use it to add believable detail but keep it secondary to characters and story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t let fascination with facts overshadow the narrative—treat research as 'spices' to finish the dish. Exceptions exist (authors like Hailey, Michener, Clancy), but for most writers, story should lead and research support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid flashback-heavy in medias res openings as a general preference
rubrics_metrics.description: In medias res often necessitates flashbacks, which the author finds clumsy, boring, and corny; he prefers starting at 'square one' and moving A-to-Z.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While recognizing brilliant counterexamples, the advice is to favor straightforward beginnings that put reader on equal footing with the writer and avoid over-reliance on swimmy flashback devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for over-explanation and under-explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful not to overexplain (which bores) or underexplain (which confuses) elements of plot, backstory, or character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Ideal Reader and feedback to identify places you’ve told too much or too little. Revise to clarify only what's necessary for the story's effect without spoon-feeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe reader behavior to judge engagement (when they put the book down)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use observed reader actions (e.g., when a reader puts the manuscript down) as diagnostic data about pacing and engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask which scene was being read when they stopped and why; use this to tighten or rework problematic sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to cut material your Ideal Reader finds boring
rubrics_metrics.description: If your key reader flags parts as boring (even if you like them), be willing to reduce or remove them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: long community-service passages were cut from two pages to two paragraphs because the Ideal Reader found them irrelevant to the emotional core. Trust ruthlessness when it improves focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark and symbol pages needing cuts during read-through
rubrics_metrics.description: Use visible markers (e.g., big symbols in the manuscript) to indicate pages requiring cuts or changes so you can find and address them in revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make concrete margin notes (e.g., 'p. 91: Sandy filches a buck — why?') that remind you to check motivation, consult notes, or make edits later.
